readings.title: A public kiosk with fewer steps
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A town installed a touchscreen kiosk for paying small service fees. Staff expected it to shorten queues, but many visitors still asked for help. The central difficulty was too many choices on the first screen. The menu displayed technical names for several services and sent people back to the beginning if they chose the wrong one. The organizers knew that a tidy plan in an office might not match what happened in an ordinary week.

The group first tried a guided task with first-time users. Staff asked visitors to complete a sample payment and recorded where they hesitated without touching the screen for them. They therefore listened to people who used the place at different times, including those who seldom attended formal meetings.

The trial showed the first choice caused the longest delay. Most users could enter details correctly after choosing a service, but the starting menu made that choice uncertain. In response, the group adopted plain labels and a visible back button. The team changed service names to everyday language and let visitors return to the previous step without losing their entries. The notes did not remove every disagreement, but they made the reasons for the next decision easier to explain.

The broader lesson was clear: simple paths matter more than extra features. The kiosk became useful when the route through a basic task matched the words and expectations of ordinary visitors. Keeping a record of small changes also helped the team distinguish a temporary setback from a lasting problem. For the people involved in a public kiosk with fewer steps, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: An alert that people noticed too late
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A coastal town sent phone alerts when a walking path closed after storms. Some walkers learned of the closure only after reaching the gate. The central difficulty was alerts delivered after journeys had begun. The message system worked, but staff entered closure details only when a worker arrived at the path. A first impression was not enough to tell the whole story, because different people approached the service in different ways.

The group first tried a review of decision and message times. The team compared weather warnings, closure decisions and phone delivery records to locate the delay. The team compared comments with direct observations rather than assuming that the loudest opinion represented everyone.

The trial showed the decision process was slower than delivery. Once staff entered an alert it reached phones quickly; the main problem was waiting too long to confirm a closure. In response, the group adopted an earlier warning with a clear update time. The town began sending a provisional notice when conditions looked unsafe and promised to confirm the status by a stated hour. Some suggestions were inexpensive, while others would have required a change to staffing or equipment.

The broader lesson was clear: timely information needs timely decisions. Faster software alone would not help walkers if the people operating the service waited until journeys were underway. The final proposal remained open to revision when new information became available. For the people involved in an alert that people noticed too late, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: A form that works on a small phone
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents could request repairs through a council website. The form looked clear on office computers but was difficult to finish on older phones. The central difficulty was important fields hidden below the screen. A long list required repeated scrolling, and an error message at the top did not identify the field that needed changing. Several participants valued the original aim even though they questioned the first method chosen to reach it.

The group first tried phone-based trials with common tasks. Designers asked residents to submit sample repair requests on different devices and listened when they described confusing steps. Short conversations after the activity revealed details that a written form had failed to capture.

The trial showed users abandoned forms after unclear errors. Most could enter the address, but they thought the form had failed when a missing date sent them back to the top. In response, the group adopted short sections and errors beside fields. The council broke the form into smaller steps and placed each correction message next to the relevant question. The people responsible made their limits clear and invited others to describe any unintended effects.

The broader lesson was clear: accessibility includes ordinary device conditions. A service available online is not fully usable if people cannot complete it on the phones they actually own. This approach gave the group a practical basis for its next round of work. For the people involved in a form that works on a small phone, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: Lending tablets through a library
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A library began lending tablets to adults taking short courses. The devices were popular, but returning borrowers often needed technical help. The central difficulty was borrowers lacked support after taking devices home. The printed guide explained how to switch on a tablet but not how to connect to a course or recover from a lost password. The project began on a small scale so that its organizers could learn before making a permanent commitment.

The group first tried a short orientation before each loan. Librarians showed borrowers basic settings and asked them to open the course page while still at the desk. They noted both benefits and costs, including the time that volunteers or staff needed to give.

The trial showed early practice prevented many later calls. Users who completed the first course login during orientation were more confident when studying independently. In response, the group adopted a help hour and clearer return guidance. The library kept loan rules simple while adding weekly assistance for problems that a short guide could not cover. The public summary described what had changed and what questions had not yet been answered.

The broader lesson was clear: access to devices includes access to support. The programme worked better when it offered the knowledge needed to use a tablet, not just the tablet itself. Readers could therefore judge the decision by its evidence rather than by a promise of perfect results. For the people involved in lending tablets through a library, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Putting a public service on a screen does not automatically make it easy to use. A town installed a payment kiosk with many choices on its first page. Visitors often selected the wrong service and had to start again. Staff asked first-time users to complete a sample task while explaining where they hesitated. They learned that the first choice caused more trouble than entering personal details later. The town replaced technical labels with everyday words and added a clear way to return to the previous step. The change reduced requests for help. A useful digital service should follow the path people actually take through a task.
translation.explanation: 注意while伴随关系和比较结构more...than。
translation.referenceAnswer: 把公共服务放到屏幕上，并不会自动让它容易使用。一个城镇安装了缴费终端，但首页有太多选项。访客常选错服务，不得不重新开始。工作人员请初次使用者完成一项模拟任务，同时说明他们在哪些步骤犹豫。工作人员发现，最初的选择比后续填写个人资料造成更多困难。城镇用日常用语替换技术标签，并增加了清楚的返回上一步方式。改动减少了求助次数。好用的数字服务应当符合人们实际完成任务的路径。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a service centre suggesting how its payment kiosk could be easier for first-time users. Describe a small user trial and two possible interface changes.
writing.explanation: 范文覆盖新用户任务观察、菜单用词与返回功能。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Service Centre Manager,
I have seen visitors hesitate at the payment kiosk before they even begin entering details. I suggest asking a few people who have never used it to complete a sample payment while staff observe quietly. We should record which menu names they choose, where they go back, and whether they know when the payment is complete. Their words will be more useful than a staff member guessing what seems clear.
Two small changes may help. First, replace technical service names with the words visitors use at the counter. Second, add a visible back button that does not erase information already entered. After making these changes, the centre could repeat the same sample task with new users and compare the number of requests for help.
Yours sincerely,
A visitor
